title: Stellar titans of Pismis 24
caption: The star cluster Pismis 24 in the nebula NGC 6357, imaged by the Danish 1.54-meter telescope at La Silla
celestial: Pismis 24 · constellation Scorpius · about 8000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESO/IDA/Danish 1.5 m/ R. Gendler, U.G. Jørgensen, J. Skottfelt, K. Harpsøe

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Blazing at the heart of NGC 6357, a nebula in Scorpius, the Scorpion, is the open star cluster Pismis 24. The surrounding clouds take on strange shapes and give the image a hazy look.

Pismis 24 is home to some of the largest stars ever found. Several of its members weigh more than 100 times the mass of the Sun. These huge, hot stars pour out enormous amounts of fierce radiation, and it is that radiation that sculpts the odd shapes of the surrounding clouds.

The nebula also keeps secrets. Its gas and dust hide huge young stars from telescopes that observe in visible light, and they add to the haze across the picture. The image was made through three visible-light filters, B, V and R, with the Danish 1.5-meter telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. Seeing the hidden young stars would require wavelengths that pass through dust more easily.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (13.59 x 13.43 arcminutes) and distance (8000 light years), the frame spans roughly 32 × 31 light-years. Its light set out about 8,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The Danish 1.54-meter telescope's DFOSC camera imaged the scene through blue (B), visual (V) and red (R) filters in visible light. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: This is visible light, but the camera's exposures gather far more of it than the eye. Even so, dust hides some young stars from view.
